results.title: RCW 19.373, Washington My Health My Data Act (official WA Legislature text)
results.snippet: Primary statute. States its intent: extra disclosures and consumer consent before collecting, sharing or using health data; a right to have health data deleted; no selling of consumer health data without a signed authorization. On a deletion request, the entity must tell every affiliate, processor, contractor and third party it shared data with, and they must delete it too. The full text also defines 'consumer', 'consumer health data' and the consent rules, which matter for data a caregiver types in about a parent or partner.

results.title: NRS Chapter 603A, Security and Privacy of Personal Information (Nevada, includes SB 370 consumer health data sections)
results.snippet: Official Nevada code. NRS 603A.400 onward (added by SB 370, 2023) requires 'affirmative, voluntary consent of the consumer' before collecting or sharing consumer health data, a health-data privacy policy (603A.500), a way to withdraw consent, deletion on request (603A.515), and rules on selling health data. Earlier sections of the same chapter (603A.010-.290) set general security and breach-notice rules.

results.title: The Connecticut Data Privacy Act (Connecticut Attorney General)
results.snippet: AG page explaining the CTDPA, including the consumer health data rules added in 2023. Says the consumer health data rules apply to any 'Consumer Health Data Controller' doing business in Connecticut or targeting Connecticut residents (not only large companies), with consent required to process or sell consumer health data. Links to AG enforcement reports (2024 and 2026) that show how the AG reads these rules.

results.title: California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA), California Attorney General
results.snippet: AG's official FAQ on the CCPA as amended by the CPRA. Covers the right to know, delete, correct, opt out of sale or sharing, and the right to limit use and disclosure of sensitive personal information (which includes health information) to what is needed to provide the service. Explains which businesses the CCPA covers (size and revenue thresholds), which matters for a small startup app.

results.snippet: This is the primary source: the 2024 final rule text of 16 CFR Part 318. It defines vendor of personal health records, PHR related entity and 'unsecured'. Use this text to decide whether a caregiver app that is not covered by HIPAA is a 'vendor of personal health records'.

results.title: Complying with FTC's Health Breach Notification Rule
results.snippet: FTC business guidance. Each affected person must be told 'without unreasonable delay' and no later than 60 calendar days after the breach is found. It covers notices to the FTC (at the same time for 500 or more people, and yearly for fewer than 500) and to the media. It also says sharing health data without the consumer's consent is a breach. Includes Q&A on who is covered.

results.title: FTC Finalizes Changes to the Health Breach Notification Rule (April 26, 2024)
results.snippet: FTC press release on the 2024 changes. It says the rule now clearly applies to health apps and similar technologies that HIPAA does not cover. It confirms that unauthorized disclosure counts as a breach. Notices must now name the third parties that got the data. The rule took effect 60 days after it was published in the Federal Register.

results.title: Collecting, Using, or Sharing Consumer Health Information? Look to HIPAA, the FTC Act, and the Health Breach Notification Rule
results.snippet: FTC guidance that sets HIPAA, FTC Act Section 5 and the HBNR side by side for health app developers. It answers angles 1 and 2 together: which law applies to an app sold straight to consumers and outside HIPAA. It also confirms that a company's own unauthorized disclosure is a breach of security.

results.title: FTC Gives Final Approval to Order Banning BetterHelp from Sharing Sensitive Health Data for Advertising
results.snippet: A Section 5 case: BetterHelp paid $7.8 million and may no longer share health data for advertising. The order requires 'affirmative express consent' before sharing with third parties, a full privacy program, and deletion of data third parties received. It also sets a data retention schedule. These show the security and consent controls the FTC expects.

results.title: Ovulation Tracking App Premom Will be Barred from Sharing Health Data for Advertising (Easy Healthcare)
results.snippet: This was the FTC's second HBNR enforcement action, after GoodRx (Feb 2023, which this release links to). Premom shared health data through third-party SDKs without users' affirmative express consent. It also failed to encrypt that data and did not notify users. The order limits how long data is kept and requires asking third parties to delete what they received. Flo Health (2021, Section 5) is summarized in the FTC 2023 Privacy and Data Security Update PDF at https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/2024.03.21-PrivacyandDataSecurityUpdate-508.pdf.

results.title: Personal Representatives (45 CFR 164.502(g)) | HHS.gov
results.snippet: Primary HHS guidance. A person authorized under state law to make health care decisions for an adult (health care POA, court-appointed guardian, or durable/general POA that includes health decisions) is the 'personal representative' and must be treated as the individual. A limited POA covers only the related information. Has an abuse/neglect/endangerment exception. Note: this binds covered entities, not a direct-to-consumer app.

results.title: Does having a health care power of attorney (POA) allow access to the patient's records under HIPAA? | HHS.gov FAQ
results.snippet: Primary HHS FAQ. A health care POA in effect makes the named person the personal representative. Some POAs take effect only when the patient loses capacity and stop if capacity returns, which matters for dementia caregivers. Providers may refuse to treat someone as representative if abuse or endangerment is suspected.

results.snippet: Primary HHS OCR guidance. When a consumer picks an app herself and types in her own data, with no doctor or health plan involved, HHS says the developer is not a HIPAA business associate. results.snippet: Primary HHS guidance on the personal representative rule. A person with authority under state law to make health care decisions for an individual (for example a healthcare power of attorney or a guardian) is treated as that individual for HIPAA rights, such as access to records. The guidance covers when a representative may be refused, for example when abuse is suspected. results.title: Summary of the HIPAA Privacy Rule (HHS.gov)

claims.claim: The CTDPA applies only to controllers that in the prior calendar year processed personal data of at least 100,000 consumers, or 25,000 consumers while deriving over 25% of gross revenue from selling personal data; it also exempts nonprofits and HIPAA-covered entities at the entity level.
claims.quote: having controlled or processed the personal data of at least (1) 100,000 consumers or (2) 25,000 consumers

claims.claim: CTDPA has no private right of action; only the Attorney General enforces it, as a CUTPA unfair trade practice with civil penalties up to $5,000 per willful violation, and the 60-day right to cure ended January 1, 2025.
claims.quote: entities may face civil penalties up to $5,000 per willful violation of the law.

claims.claim: Connecticut's separate breach notice statute (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 36a-701b(b)(1)) requires notice to the AG and affected residents without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after discovery, which the AG counts from when a company becomes aware of suspicious activity.
claims.quote: without unreasonable delay, but not later than sixty (60) days after breach discovery

claims.claim: The CCPA covers only for-profit businesses doing business in California that meet one of these tests: gross annual revenue over $25 million; buying, selling or sharing personal information of 100,000 or more California residents or households; or making 50% or more of annual revenue from selling California residents' personal information. claims.quote: Have a gross annual revenue of over $25 million

claims.quote: information concerning a consumer’s health, sex life, or sexual orientation

claims.claim: A covered business must answer a consumer's request to know or delete within 45 calendar days. claims.quote: Businesses must respond to your request within 45 calendar days.

claims.quote: No. Developer is not creating, receiving, maintaining or transmitting protected health information (PHI) on behalf of a covered entity

claims.quote: The consumer’s use of an app to transmit data to a covered entity does not by itself make the app developer a BA

claims.claim: OCR says a developer becomes a business associate, and HIPAA applies, when a provider or health plan contracts with it to create, receive, maintain or transmit PHI. claims.quote: as long as the developer keeps the health information attached to these two versions of the app separate

claims.quote: Does the consumer control all decisions about whether to transmit her data to a third party

claims.quote: the Privacy Rule at 45 CFR 164.502(g) requires covered entities to treat an individual's personal representative as the individual

claims.claim: For an adult, the personal representative is someone with legal authority to make health care decisions for that person. claims.quote: A person with legal authority to make health care decisions on behalf of the individual

claims.quote: the personal representative is to be treated as the individual only with respect to protected health information that is relevant to the representation

claims.quote: family members or other persons who are involved in the individual's health care or payment for care may receive protected health information

claims.quote: applies to certain businesses or organizations that aren't covered by HIPAA – specifically, vendors of personal health records (PHR), PHR related entities, and third party service providers.

claims.claim: The FTC expects companies handling health data to keep a written security program, set data retention/purpose/use limits, ensure consent is meaningful and informed, and avoid claiming to be 'HIPAA Compliant' or 'HIPAA Certified' when misleading; health information is defined broadly to include anything enabling an inference about health.
claims.quote: don't make false or misleading claims that you are "HIPAA Compliant," "HIPAA Secure," "HIPAA Certified" or the like.

claims.claim: Washington's My Health My Data Act covers personal health data that HIPAA does not cover. Its purpose is to stop a consumer's health data from being collected and shared without that consumer's consent.
claims.quote: protect a consumer's sensitive health data from being collected and shared without that consumer's consent

claims.claim: The Act applies to an out-of-state business that serves Washington consumers and decides how consumer health data is collected, processed, shared or sold. claims.quote: Out-of-state entities that are processors for regulated entities or a small business must comply with the Act.

claims.claim: Under section 6, consumers can have their health data deleted from a regulated entity's network, including archives and backups. Under section 9, selling health data needs the consumer's valid authorization, and both seller and buyer must keep a copy for six years.
claims.quote: have their consumer health data deleted from a regulated entity's or small business' network, including archived or backup systems

claims.claim: Regulated entities and small businesses must post a separate link to a consumer health data privacy policy on their homepage. Any violation of the Act is a per se violation of the Washington Consumer Protection Act, enforced by the Attorney General and through private lawsuits.
claims.quote: shall prominently publish a link to its consumer health data privacy policy on its homepage

claims.claim: Compliance dates: section 10 for all persons from July 23, 2023; sections 4 to 9 from March 31, 2024 for regulated entities and from June 30, 2024 for small businesses. claims.quote: an app that tracks someone's digestion or perspiration is collecting consumer health data

claims.claim: Under HIPAA, a person named in a health care power of attorney that is currently in effect is generally the patient's personal representative.
claims.quote: If a health care power of attorney is currently in effect, the named person would be the patient's personal representative

claims.claim: Whether a health care POA is in effect depends on its type. Some take effect right away. Others start only when the patient cannot make health care decisions, and they end if the patient regains that capacity.
claims.quote: others are only triggered if and when the patient lacks the capacity to make health care decisions

claims.quote: HIPAA provides a personal representative of a patient with the same rights to access health information as the patient

claims.claim: The exceptions to the patient's right of access also apply to the personal representative. For example, a psychotherapist's separately kept session notes are not covered by the HIPAA right of access.
claims.quote: a psychotherapist's separate notes of counseling sessions, kept separately from the patient chart, are not included

claims.claim: Under 45 CFR 164.502(g)(5), a provider may refuse to treat someone as the personal representative if the provider believes the patient has been or may be subject to violence, abuse or neglect by that person, or would be endangered, and judges that doing so is not in the patient's best interests.

claims.quote: Such protections are sometimes required by federal and state laws, including the HIPAA Privacy, Security, and Breach Notification Rules.

claims.quote: These include the FTC Act, the FTC’s Health Breach Notification Rule, the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) Rules

claims.claim: HHS points to a separate PDF, 'Health App Use Scenarios & HIPAA' (February 2016), as its guidance on when an app developer acts as a HIPAA business associate. That PDF is the primary source to read next for angle 1.
claims.quote: explains when an app developer may be acting as a business associate under the HIPAA Rules

claims.claim: The tool asks about what the app does, what data it collects and what services it provides. Which law applies depends on those facts, so a law cannot be picked from the app type alone.
claims.quote: asks developers a series of questions about the nature of their app, including about its function, the data it collects

claims.claim: OCR has published separate guidance on HIPAA and cloud computing for covered entities, business associates and cloud service providers. It applies to hosting choices such as Vercel and Supabase only if HIPAA applies.
claims.quote: OCR developed guidance to assist HIPAA covered entities and business associates, including cloud services providers (CSPs)

claims.claim: HIPAA Rules do not apply to health information held by an entity that is not a covered entity or business associate; a consumer app not offered by a covered entity or its business associate likely falls outside HIPAA, even if the data came from a covered entity.
claims.quote: the HIPAA Rules likely wouldn't apply to consumer health information maintained in an app that isn't offered by a HIPAA covered entity or its business associate

claims.claim: The FTC Health Breach Notification Rule applies to most health apps not covered by HIPAA, because app developers are treated as 'health care providers' under 42 U.S.C. 1320d as referenced in 16 CFR 318.2(e).
claims.quote: applies to most health apps that aren't covered by HIPAA because most developers of health apps are acting as "health care providers"

claims.claim: Under the HBNR, a breach includes unauthorized sharing of identifying health information without consumer authorization, and triggers notice to consumers, the FTC, and in some cases the media, with civil penalties for failing to notify.
claims.quote: any incidents of unauthorized access, including sharing of identifying health information, without consumers' authorization

claims.claim: FTC Act Section 5 applies to most app developers, including health apps, and requires reasonable privacy and security practices; sharing health data with third parties after promising privacy can violate it.
claims.quote: there's a good chance the FTC Act will require you, among other things, to have reasonable privacy and security practices in place

claims.claim: The FTC tool is informational only, not legal advice, and using it cannot guarantee compliance, so legal review is still needed.
claims.quote: This tool is not offering legal advice and is provided for informational purposes only.

claims.claim: Nevada SB 370 bars a regulated entity from collecting consumer health data without the consumer's affirmative consent. The one exception is data needed to provide a product or service that the person the data is about has requested. Sharing needs a second consent, separate from the consent to collect. For a caregiver app this matters because the data is about the parent or partner, not the user who signs up.
claims.quote: With the affirmative consent of the consumer to whom the consumer health data relates, which must be separate and distinct

claims.claim: Consent under SB 370 must be an affirmative, voluntary act. It cannot come from accepting general terms of use, from hovering over or closing content, or from a dark-pattern interface. The consent request must name the data categories, the purpose, who the data is shared with, and how to withdraw consent.
claims.quote: may not be provided through: 1. The acceptance of a general agreement concerning terms of use

claims.claim: On request, a regulated entity must confirm what data it collects, list the third parties it shares with, stop collecting, or delete the data. It must answer within 45 days of authenticating the request, with one 45-day extension allowed. Deletion is due within 30 days, and the entity must notify its processors, which then have 30 days to delete. Data on backups may wait up to 6 months.
claims.quote: Not later than 30 days after authenticating a request ... for the deletion of consumer health data

claims.claim: SB 370 Section 28 limits which employees, processors and contractors may access consumer health data, and only for necessary purposes. It also requires administrative, technical and physical security policies that meet the industry standard of care and NRS 603A. Processors may handle the data only under a written contract.
claims.quote: establish, implement and maintain policies and practices for the administrative, technical and physical security of consumer health data

claims.claim: SB 370 defines consumer health data broadly. It covers any health condition or diagnosis, behavioral interventions, medication use, and symptoms. This would cover the dementia and behavior details caregivers type in. The definition is limited to people who live in Nevada or whose data is collected in Nevada.
claims.quote: related to the past, present or future health of the consumer

claims.claim: Under 45 CFR 164.502(g)(2), a covered entity must treat a person who has legal authority to make health care decisions for an adult (such as a health care power of attorney or a health care proxy) as that adult's personal representative. claims.quote: If under applicable law a person has authority to act on behalf of an individual who is an adult or an emancipated minor in making decisions related to health care, a covered entity must treat such person as a personal representative

claims.quote: If under applicable law a person has authority to act on behalf of an individual ... in making decisions related to health care

claims.quote: The individual has been or may be subjected to domestic violence, abuse, or neglect by such person.

claims.claim: Covered entities must keep protecting a deceased person's PHI for 50 years after death. An executor or administrator with legal authority over the estate is treated as the personal representative.
claims.quote: for a period of 50 years following the death of the individual

claims.quote: means a natural person who has requested a product or service from a regulated entity and who resides in this State or whose consumer health data is collected in this State

claims.quote: shall establish, implement and maintain policies and practices for the administrative, technical and physical security of consumer health data

claims.claim: NRS 603A.535 bars selling, or offering to sell, consumer health data without the written authorization of the consumer the data is about. It also bars making a product or service conditional on agreeing to such a sale.

claims.claim: Under the amended rule, a 'breach of security' is not only a hack: an unauthorized disclosure (for example, sharing health data without the person's authorization) also counts, and unauthorized access is presumed to be acquisition unless the company has reliable evidence otherwise.
claims.quote: A breach of security includes an unauthorized acquisition of unsecured PHR identifiable health information in a personal health record that occurs as a result of a data breach or an unauthorized disclosure.

claims.claim: The rule's coverage reaches non-HIPAA apps and websites: 'health care services or supplies' is defined to include any website or mobile app that tracks health conditions, medications, symptoms, mental health, and similar items, which makes such app makers 'covered health care providers' whose data can be PHR identifiable health information.

claims.claim: A 'vendor of personal health records' is any non-HIPAA-covered entity (and not acting as a business associate) that offers or maintains an electronic health record about an individual that can draw information from multiple sources and is managed, shared and controlled by or primarily for the individual.
claims.quote: Personal health record (PHR) means an electronic record of PHR identifiable health information on an individual that has the technical capacity to draw information from multiple sources and that is managed, shared, and controlled by or primarily for the individual.

claims.claim: After a breach, the vendor must notify affected individuals, the FTC, and (when 500+ residents of a state are affected) prominent media; FTC notice for breaches of 500+ people must be contemporaneous with individual notice, while breaches under 500 can be logged and reported to the FTC annually within 60 days after year end. claims.quote: All logged notifications required under § 318.5(c) (regarding notice to FTC) involving the unsecured PHR identifiable health information of fewer than 500 individuals may be sent annually to the Federal Trade Commission no later than 60 calendar days following the end of the calendar year.

claims.claim: Data counts as 'unsecured' (and so triggers the rule) unless it is protected by a technology or method named in HHS guidance under 42 U.S.C. 17932(h)(2), which ties the rule's breach exposure to encryption/destruction standards set by HHS; violations are treated as violations of an FTC Act section 18 trade regulation rule.
claims.quote: Unsecured means PHR identifiable information that is not protected through the use of a technology or methodology specified by the Secretary of Health and Human Services

result.summary: HHS's own guidance says HIPAA is "not likely" to apply to an app that serves consumers directly and is not working for a doctor, hospital, health plan or clearinghouse. HHS also says the answer depends on the facts. The FTC rules still apply. The FTC Act Section 5 covers companies that handle health data outside HIPAA. Since its 2024 changes, the FTC Health Breach Notification Rule also reaches health apps that keep a personal health record. Under that rule, sharing someone's health data without their permission counts as a breach, just like a hack. It sets deadlines: notify people within 60 days, notify the FTC, and notify the media when 500 or more people in one state are affected. State laws add consent rules. Washington's My Health My Data Act and Nevada's SB 370 require opt-in consent before collecting health data, and a second, separate consent before sharing it. Both tie these rights to the person the data is about, which here is the parent or partner. Nevada also sets deadlines for deletion requests. Connecticut's law covers any business that controls consumer health data, no matter how small. Whether the app counts as a 'vendor of personal health records' or a 'regulated entity' is still an open legal question. So is whose consent counts when a caregiver enters another person's data. A qualified lawyer must answer both. This research does not say the product is compliant or not covered.

findings.claim: HIPAA probably does not apply to a direct-to-consumer app, but the answer depends on the facts. HHS OCR says an app that serves only consumers, and not a provider, health plan or clearinghouse, is 'not likely' to be a covered entity or business associate. In its example of a consumer entering her own data, the developer is not a business associate. HHS says HIPAA protections are 'sometimes' required, and that a change in facts (such as a covered entity paying or contracting with the developer) can change the answer.
findings.evidence: The 2016 OCR scenarios PDF, page 3 (Key Questions), says such an app is 'not likely to be subject to HIPAA as either a covered entity or business associate'. In the page 1-2 scenario, the answer to whether the developer is a business associate is 'No'. The HHS health apps page says protections are 'sometimes required' by HIPAA. Limit: the scenarios cover a consumer entering her OWN data. They do not cover a caregiver entering data about another person.

findings.claim: Several federal laws may apply, and the FTC, OCR, ONC and FDA offer a tool that helps sort out which ones. The Mobile Health Apps Interactive Tool points developers to the FTC Act, the FTC Health Breach Notification Rule, HIPAA, the FD&C Act, COPPA, and the 21st Century Cures Act with the ONC information blocking rules.
findings.evidence: The HHS page lists these laws as ones that 'might apply'. The tool itself is on ftc.gov. It was not run for this product.

findings.claim: FTC Act Section 5 (unfair or deceptive practices) applies to companies that collect, use or share health data even when HIPAA does not apply. So a for-profit direct-to-consumer caregiving app falls under FTC enforcement power. The FTC brought cases against GoodRx, BetterHelp and Flo, all consumer health apps outside HIPAA.
findings.evidence: The FTC guidance quote is word for word: obligations apply to companies 'that aren't required to comply with HIPAA'. Confidence is medium because the GoodRx, BetterHelp and Flo case pages were not fetched; those cases come from the verifier's recall. Nonprofits may fall outside FTC Section 5. Being under FTC enforcement power is not a finding of any violation.

findings.claim: The FTC Health Breach Notification Rule (16 CFR Part 318, amended 2024, in effect July 29, 2024) covers non-HIPAA vendors of personal health records (PHRs), PHR related entities, and their third-party service providers, such as data storage companies. A PHR is an electronic record of identifiable health information that can draw information from more than one source and is managed, shared and controlled 'by or primarily for the individual'. The 2024 changes say outright that health apps are meant to be covered. The rule defines 'health care services or supplies' to include any website or app that tracks conditions, medications, symptoms or mental health. In September 2026 the FTC withdrew its older 2021 policy statement because the 2024 rule already covers health apps.
findings.evidence: The definitions were checked word for word in eCFR 16 CFR 318.2. Open questions for a lawyer: (a) whether this app can 'draw information from multiple sources' (if only caregivers type data in, it may not), and (b) whether a record a caregiver keeps about a parent counts as kept 'primarily for the individual'. Third-party service providers must notify the vendor, not consumers.

findings.claim: Under the rule, a 'breach of security' covers more than hacking. It includes the company's own sharing of identifiable health information without the person's permission, for example sending health data with identifiers to an ad network or social media platform. Unauthorized access is presumed to be acquisition unless the company has reliable evidence otherwise. The rule covers only 'unsecured' data, meaning data not protected by HHS-specified methods (encryption or destruction).
findings.evidence: In the 16 CFR 318.2 definition, a breach 'occurs as a result of a data breach or an unauthorized disclosure', and access is presumed to be acquisition. In FTC guidance: 'sharing of covered information without an individual's authorization, trigger[s] notification obligations', with a social-media example. Why this matters here: relatives seeing data, or analytics and tracking tools on the page, could count as sharing. That inference is not tested.

findings.claim: Breach deadlines: notify each affected person without unreasonable delay, and no later than 60 calendar days after the breach is discovered. Waiting until day 60 can still be unreasonable. For breaches of 500 or more people, notify the FTC at the same time as the individuals. For fewer than 500, keep a log and send it to the FTC within 60 days after the calendar year ends. Notify prominent media when 500 or more residents of one state, D.C. or a US territory are affected. Email and other electronic notice are allowed, and they must be clear and conspicuous. Required content is set in § 318.6. Law enforcement can ask for a delay (§ 318.4(d)).
findings.evidence: The deadlines match the eCFR rule text and the FTC guidance updated 2026-07-14. The 2024 rule replaced the old 10-business-day FTC deadline.

findings.claim: Washington My Health My Data Act (RCW 19.373): collecting consumer health data needs consent for a stated purpose, unless the data is needed to provide a service the consumer asked for. Sharing needs a SEPARATE consent from the collection consent, with the same exception. Consent must come before collecting or sharing. The request must clearly show the data categories, the purpose and specific uses, the categories of recipients, and how to withdraw consent. Consent must be a clear opt-in act. Accepting broad terms of use, hovering, closing content, or deceptive designs do not count. The Act was written to cover apps HIPAA does not cover. Consumer health data includes conditions, diagnoses, behavioral interventions and medication. Collection and sharing consent belong to the consumer 'to whom such consumer health data relates', and the deletion right is about data 'concerning the consumer'. Large entities had to comply from March 31, 2024, and small businesses from June 30, 2024.
findings.vote: 3-0 for the consent rules (claims 18, 19); 2-1 for the scope and whose-rights reading (claim 20)
findings.evidence: Statute text fetched 2026-11-12. One verifier dissented on claim 20. The verified note is that the phrase 'to whom ... relates' sits in the consent and access sections, not in the deletion section. 'Consumer' means a Washington resident, or a person whose data is collected in Washington, acting in an individual or household context. Why this matters here: the person the data is about is the parent or partner, not the caregiver who signed up. How consent works in that case needs a lawyer.

findings.claim: Nevada SB 370 (NRS 603A.400 et seq., in effect March 31, 2024): collecting consumer health data needs affirmative, voluntary consent unless it is needed for a requested service. Sharing needs a separate consent 'of the consumer to whom the consumer health data relates', unless it is needed for a requested service or another law requires or allows it. Consent must come first and must show the data categories, the purpose, the categories of recipients, and how to withdraw. A 'consumer' is a person who requested a product or service and lives in Nevada, or whose data is collected there. That leaves open whether a parent or partner who never signed up is protected. On request, the business must confirm whether it collects, shares or sells the data, list the third parties, stop collecting or sharing, and delete. It must respond within 45 days of verifying the request, with one 45-day extension allowed. It must delete within 30 days and tell affiliates, processors, contractors and third parties, who then have 30 days to delete. Backup copies may wait up to 2 years, only as needed to restore the backup.
findings.evidence: Official statute fetched 2026-11-12. The definition of consumer health data also requires that the business uses the data to identify the consumer's health status. Whose consent counts for data about a non-user is a question for a lawyer.

findings.claim: Under the Connecticut Data Privacy Act, any business that controls consumer health data and does business in Connecticut, or targets Connecticut residents, is covered no matter its size or how much data it handles. The nonprofit exemption does not apply to these businesses. A small caregiving app could be covered starting with its first Connecticut user.
findings.evidence: The Attorney General's page says there are 'no revenue or processing thresholds that a Consumer Health Data Controller must meet'. Confidence is medium because there is only one source, an Attorney General summary page, and the statute text and its consent and deletion rules were not read. The 'first user' part is an inference and depends on doing business in Connecticut.
